questions.title: How exactly does the sLSTM 'memory mixing' differ from standard RNN hidden-to-hidden connections?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the distinction made in Section 2 regarding 'new memory mixing'. The paper mentions that sLSTM has recurrent connections ($\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{i}}, \dots$) from the hidden state vector $\mathbf{h}$ to the memory cell inputs and gates. In standard LSTMs (Equation 3), we already have $r_z h_{t-1}$ terms. What makes the sLSTM's memory mixing 'new' or distinct enough to claim it solves state tracking problems while mLSTM cannot? Is it purely due to the interaction with the exponential gating?

questions.title: Is the normalizer state $n_t$ in sLSTM mathematically equivalent to a running average of input gates?
questions.question_body: Looking at Equation 4 for sLSTM, the normalizer state is defined as $n_t = f_t n_{t-1} + i_t$. If we expand this recursively, it looks like a weighted sum of all previous input gates, where the weights are products of subsequent forget gates. Does this effectively act as a cumulative count of 'active' input events over time? If so, why is division by this scalar necessary to prevent saturation when using exponential gating instead of sigmoid?

questions.title: Does the covariance update rule in mLSTM imply that the model implicitly implements a form of attention without explicit token-token interactions?
questions.question_body: The mLSTM uses a matrix memory updated via $\mathbf{C}_t = f_t \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top$. When retrieving, it computes $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t$. This looks like a dot-product similarity search where all past $(\mathbf{k}, \mathbf{v})$ pairs are summed into $\mathbf{C}$. Why does this avoid the quadratic complexity of Self-Attention? Specifically, if I have a sequence length $T$, isn't computing $\sum_{j=1}^T v_j k_j^T q$ still requiring access to all past elements? How is this operation truly linear in $T$ during inference?

questions.title: What is the precise role of the stabilizer state $m_t$ in preventing numerical overflow with exponential gates?
questions.question_body: In Equation 5, the paper introduces a stabilizer state $m_t = \max(\log(f_t) + m_{t-1}, \log(i_t))$ and defines stabilized gates using subtraction from this max value. Intuitively, this seems like implementing a log-sum-exp trick or shifting for numerical stability. However, since we subtract $m_t$, doesn't this just shift all probabilities down uniformly? How does ensuring bounded values here actually help with *training* convergence compared to simply clipping values or using softplus activations initially?

questions.title: If mLSTM is fully parallelizable, why does its wall-clock time suffer compared to FlashAttention despite theoretical speedups?
questions.question_body: Section 3 claims mLSTM is fully parallelizable and comparable to FlashAttention. However, Section 6 (Limitations) admits that current CUDA kernels are 'about 4 times slower than FlashAttention' because they aren't optimized yet. But beyond engineering optimization issues, isn't updating a dense $d \times d$ matrix every timestep inherently more expensive than scanning linear states (like in Mamba)? Does the $O(d^2)$ per-step cost become a bottleneck for very large dimensions even with perfect parallelization?

questions.title: How does xLSTM reconcile the conflicting requirements of 'state tracking' (requiring recurrence) and 'parallelizability' (required for efficiency)?
questions.question_body: The abstract highlights that xLSTM combines sLSTM (with memory mixing/state tracking) and mLSTM (fully parallelizable). The paper states that sLSTM is not parallelizable due to hidden-hidden connections. Yet, they stack them into an architecture (xLSTM[$a:b$]). If sLSTM blocks must run sequentially over time steps internally, how does stacking them alongside parallel mLSTM blocks affect overall training throughput? Is there a hybrid strategy where only certain layers use sLSTM while others remain parallel?
